As for getting the footage off the cameras, that part is relatively straightforward.

As soon as an officer places their camera on charge back at the station, their camera would authenticate with the video server and automatically sync up the footage it recorded since its last charge, along with which officer was using the camera at the time.

When the officer fills in their activity report at the end of their shift, the times of incidents the officer attended that day are sent to the video server, which flags those periods of the officer's daily footage for long-term storage.

You'd probably want a system where logged incidents are stored for a few months or until required as evidence, with all daily footage kept for a week and deleted on a rolling basis as long as the officer has no complaints filed against them.

Storage is quite affordable nowadays. Based on my own surveillance system, 8 hours of continuous 1080 footage at 30fps would come in at around 30GB. Meaning that assuming law enforcement works a 5-day week, the rolling storage you'd need would be about 150GB of storage per officer (which currently costs around £20 per terabyte).

The amount of long-term storage needed would depend on how much of an officer's time is actually spent attending incidents, which I'd imagine isn't that high overall.

"Discipline" doesn't have to mean pain. I don't think your trainer understands this.

While applying physical pain *can* work to condition a dog to do certain things, it has to be done correctly, and even when it is, it can be deeply unhealthy for the relationship between you and the dog and can lead to a fear-based relationship rather than one of love and mutual respect.

I'll readily admit that I use a small amount of discipline (as well as lots of fun and rewards) to train my dogs, but only under extreme (life & death) circumstances would I consider using physical pain to reinforce a point.

For example, a gentle short-sharp tug on a long training lead doesn't cause any actual pain and is a valid way of correcting a dog that is having issues with recall (along with praise & rewards when the dog does as it's asked). Dragging the dog about by the lead/collar half-choking it, however, doesn't teach the dog anything and is just inflicting pain for the sake of it.

---

As the dog's owner, you don't need to constantly show physical "dominance," as that will eventually just cause the dog to fear & resent you (or worse, it'll say "forget you" and just do the opposite of anything you say).

As the 'pack leader,' you do want the dog to respect you though (and it needs you to show it respect in return). You earn that respect by fulfilling the dog's needs in terms of food, shelter, love, affection, fun, sufficient exercise, and where needed... discipline.

The way I see it is if you fail to give enough of any one of those, the dog will start to fail to see you as the leader, and that's when you'll likely start to have behavioral problems.

Be proactive in speaking to your neighbors.

Explain that you've just gotten a new dog, so there may be some initial noise due to separation anxiety, but you're working to resolve it as quickly as possible. Emphasize that you are aware of the noise your dog may be making and are actively taking steps to correct it.

Here are some strategies that have worked for me in addressing separation anxiety (and that I've recommended to others with positive results):

* Place some of your worn clothing in their crate or basket so they can smell you when you're not around (avoid using your best clothes in case the dog chews them).
* Leave a radio or television on, preferably with talk shows or soothing music (not heavy metal).
* Don't make a big deal when you leave; avoid lengthy goodbyes. Depart quickly and quietly with minimal fuss and noise.
* If using a crate, put the dog in it for a while before you leave so they don't associate the crate with being left alone.
* When you return, don't give them attention until they've calmed down. As difficult as it may be, ignore them completely if necessary. This reinforces the idea that your return is linked to their calm behavior, not their excitement.
* If you leave the house and hear noise immediately, don't go back in to reassure them, as this will reinforce that behavior.
* Initially, only leave the dog alone after they've had a long walk and off-leash run to expend energy. Assuming they can hold it, tire them out first, then feed them so they have a full stomach along with being tired.
